problem_plain: A large AI model stores tens of billions of numbers. Every time the chip does any work, it must pull those numbers from memory chips across slow wires into the part of the chip that does math — and that wire journey is far slower and burns far more energy than the math itself. Using smaller, rounded numbers — say 4-bit numbers instead of 16-bit numbers — means the same wire can carry four times as much of the model per second, and the same memory chip can hold a model four times as large.
why_plain: Bandwidth — how fast data moves — is a physical wall: the wires between memory chips and the math circuits can only carry a fixed number of bits per second, and that limit has grown far more slowly than model size. Using smaller numbers means more of the model fits in the small but fast on-chip memory, so the chip makes fewer slow round-trips out to the bigger but slower memory chips.
approach_plain: Researchers replace 16-bit or 32-bit numbers with compact codes — smaller integers or entries in a lookup table — then either retrain the model so it learns to live with the rounding, or redesign the chip's math circuits to work directly in the smaller format. The hard part is that not all numbers in a model matter equally: a handful of very large 'outlier' values carry a disproportionate share of information, and simply rounding them breaks accuracy badly. Most papers therefore pair a clever compression strategy (which finds or protects those outliers) with a matched piece of hardware (which knows how to operate in the smaller format without first converting everything back to the original size).

groups.heading: Making the number format itself smarter
groups.explain: Instead of forcing every stored weight or computed value into a fixed 4-bit or 8-bit slot, these papers design number formats that adjust to whatever range of values actually appears in a given part of the model. A standard fixed grid wastes most of its available codes on values that never show up; an adaptive format places its grid lines where values actually cluster, squeezing more accuracy out of the same number of bits.

papers.name: M-ANT
papers.gloss: Picks the best number grid independently for each small group of 128 weights, then handles the model's running notes in real time using the same adaptive hardware; up to 4.46x faster than a prior leading accelerator.

papers.name: Anda
papers.gloss: Defines a new number type where each group of computed values shares one overall scale but each individual value gets a bit-length tuned to that layer's needs, all without retraining; 2.4x faster and 3.1x more energy-efficient than a standard baseline.

papers.name: MX+
papers.gloss: Fixes a flaw in an industry-standard 4-bit format: the single largest value in each 32-number block was encoded with almost no precision, causing big errors; MX+ borrows unused bits in that slot to give it proper precision, recovering up to 42 percentage points of accuracy with almost no extra storage.

papers.name: FATE
papers.gloss: Uses different number precisions for different dimensions of a pattern-matching system that works with very long binary strings, since some dimensions carry more information than others; targets low-power chips on small embedded boards.

groups.heading: Compressing the model's running notes
groups.explain: When a model reads a long document or conversation, it builds up a buffer — the model's running notes — that records what every earlier word meant in context. This buffer grows with conversation length and is re-read on every single word the model writes, so it consumes a huge share of bandwidth. Shrinking those notes from 16-bit to 4-bit numbers cuts that bandwidth cost roughly four times over, but the notes contain the same outlier problem as the model's stored weights.

papers.name: Oaken
papers.gloss: Studies each layer's note values once ahead of time to learn which values are outliers, then at run time splits each note into three groups and rounds each group to 4 or 5 bits; stores outliers in a compact side channel, shrinking their cost from 23 to 8 bits each; 1.79x more throughput than a standard server at batch size 256.

papers.name: COMET
papers.gloss: Rounds both the model's stored weights and its running notes to 4-bit numbers at the same time, keeping occasional very large values at 8 bits; a custom math routine handles both sizes in one pass; 2.88x faster inner-loop throughput and 2.02x faster end-to-end speed versus a standard serving library.

papers.name: QServe
papers.gloss: Uses a two-step rounding process — first to 8-bit, then to 4-bit — with a protected number range that guarantees no overflow when the chip does 8-bit math; folds the scaling needed for 4-bit running notes into the preceding weight matrix so no extra work is needed at run time; up to 3.5x more throughput than a vendor-optimized library on a top data-center GPU.

groups.heading: Lookup tables instead of multiply circuits
groups.explain: When weights are rounded down to 2 or 3 bits, there are so few possible values that instead of computing an input times a weight, the chip can simply look up the answer in a small table. A lookup table is far cheaper in silicon area and energy than a floating-point multiply circuit. These papers build both the training recipes and the matching hardware to make a lookup table a practical replacement for conventional arithmetic.

papers.name: LUT Tensor Core
papers.gloss: Replaces the GPU's matrix-multiply engine with a lookup table that works bit by bit: weights are re-encoded so half the table entries cancel out by symmetry, and software folds the table-building step into the previous layer to hide its cost; 2 to 5.5x faster inference end-to-end; 4 to 6x smaller chip area than a conventional multiply circuit.

papers.name: FIGLUT
papers.gloss: Pre-computes all possible products of an input value with every possible low-bit weight pattern and stores them in a half-size lookup table; at run time the hardware reads the table using the weight bits rather than multiplying; 59% better energy efficiency than a prior lookup-table chip at the same 3-bit precision.

papers.name: LUT-DLA
papers.gloss: Replaces multiply-and-add circuits entirely with lookup-table fetch-and-add circuits, trained using a multi-stage recipe; achieves sub-1-bit-equivalent compression by representing groups of values with shared dictionary entries; 1.4 to 7x better power efficiency and up to 146x better area efficiency than standard rounding hardware.

papers.name: VQ-LLM
papers.gloss: Solves why lookup-table inference was actually slower than plain 16-bit inference on GPUs: the dictionary entries were being fetched from shared memory in a way that caused threads to queue up; VQ-LLM keeps the most-used dictionary entries in each thread's private registers and reorganizes computation to avoid that bottleneck; 64 to 99% lower latency versus prior lookup-table methods.

groups.heading: Grouping weights together before compressing
groups.explain: Instead of rounding each weight number individually, this approach takes a small group of weights — say 8 or 16 at a time — and replaces the whole group with a single code pointing to the nearest matching group in a learned dictionary. The dictionary can capture patterns that span across many weights at once, achieving higher compression at the same accuracy. The main challenge is that building the dictionary requires an expensive clustering step, and wrong dictionary entries hurt accuracy badly.

papers.name: MVQ
papers.gloss: Combines skipping unimportant numbers in a regular pattern with a dictionary-building algorithm that ignores the skipped zeros so they cannot distort the dictionary; the matching hardware skips those positions in its compute array, cutting array area by 55% and improving energy efficiency by 2.3x.

papers.name: eDKM
papers.gloss: Makes dictionary-based weight compression practical for 7-billion-parameter models by removing duplicate data and splitting large temporary arrays that must be kept in main memory during training; cuts per-layer memory 130x, shrinking a 7-billion-parameter model from 12.6 GB to 2.5 GB at 3 bits per weight.

papers.name: BitMoD
papers.gloss: Gives each group of 128 weights its own number format chosen from a small family of options, and runs all format types through a single bit-by-bit hardware path rather than needing separate circuits for each format; 1.69x faster than a prior adaptive-format accelerator at under 0.5% accuracy loss.

groups.heading: Making smaller numbers work on chips that were not designed for them
groups.explain: Most chips already in use — graphics processors, ordinary processors, programmable chips — were not built to do 3-bit or 4-bit math. These papers bridge that gap by designing software routines, new chip instructions, or small hardware additions that let existing chips run models with smaller numbers efficiently, without a complete redesign of the chip.

papers.name: DECA
papers.gloss: Adds a small hardware block beside each processor core that unpacks rounded and skipped-number-format weight tiles in a three-stage pipeline, hiding that unpacking work behind a new instruction that fetches data early; on a server processor running a 70-billion-parameter model the unpacking was eating 95% of all instructions — DECA eliminates that bottleneck, giving 1.6 to 2.6x faster word-by-word output.

papers.name: CAMP
papers.gloss: Adds a small extra multiplier to standard ARM and RISC-V processor math units so they can do 4-bit and 8-bit integer matrix math natively; uses only 1 to 4% extra chip area; up to 23x faster than an unmodified processor core on rounded-number matrix math.

papers.name: HiPACK
papers.gloss: Solves the mismatch between 4-bit weights and 8-bit processor registers by pre-expanding the packed 4-bit data before the math loop, then arranging registers so one instruction can process two packed streams at once; up to 4.6x faster than a full-precision baseline on a Raspberry Pi 4.

papers.name: MEADOW
papers.gloss: Runs 8-bit rounded language model inference on a low-power 10-watt programmable chip by processing one attention head at a time rather than all at once, and packing weights so common values are fetched from fast on-chip memory; 1.5x faster word output and 2.5x faster reading-in-the-prompt than a straightforward implementation.

papers.name: MiLo
papers.gloss: Compresses a model made of specialists — where different sub-networks activate for different inputs — to 3-bit weights without any calibration data, then adds small correction layers that restore accuracy; the 3-bit math routine wastes no bits in packing and supports processing multiple requests at once, which prior 3-bit routines could not; 1.2x throughput over the previous best approach.

papers.name: HyC-LoRA
papers.gloss: Compresses the temporary value buffers stored during fine-tuning — adapting a pre-trained model to a new task — to near 2 bits on average, protecting large outlier values around non-math operations and reordering computation so some buffers can be recomputed rather than stored; targets fine-tuning on a single consumer GPU.

groups.heading: Using smaller numbers for tasks beyond language models
groups.explain: The same bandwidth wall that limits language models also affects protein structure prediction, image-generation models, 3D graphics rendering, searching large databases for similar entries, and even the electrical stability of the chip itself. Each workload has its own pattern of values and its own memory access habits, so each needs its own approach to using smaller numbers.

papers.name: LightNobel
papers.gloss: Handles the rapidly growing value arrays in protein structure prediction by sorting values by size and applying 4-bit rounding to ordinary values while keeping large outliers in 16-bit numbers; a reconfigurable hardware math unit dynamically assigns its compute lanes to each mix of precisions; 8.44x faster than a top data-center GPU on the most expensive step, with peak memory cut 120x for long protein sequences.

papers.name: Ditto
papers.gloss: Exploits the fact that neighboring steps in an image-generation model produce nearly identical outputs: the change from one step to the next is tiny and can be encoded in very few bits, often zero; a matched accelerator skips zero-change computations entirely; up to 1.5x faster with 17.7% energy savings.

papers.name: AQB8
papers.gloss: Rounds the tree of bounding boxes used in 3D ray tracing — the data structure that figures out which surfaces a light ray might hit — to 8-bit numbers at every level, so all intersection tests run in integer math with no conversion back to floating point; 1.82x faster than a standard GPU ray-tracing unit with 49% less energy and 70% fewer trips to memory chips.

papers.name: Panacea
papers.gloss: Fixes an incompatibility between offset-based rounding — which gives better accuracy — and bit-slice computation — which skips zero slices for efficiency: offset encoding produces many non-zero slices that a naive skip engine would miss; Panacea shifts the offset and picks bit slices to maximize zeros that can be skipped; 1.97x more energy-efficient than a prior bit-slice accelerator.

papers.name: NeuVSA
papers.gloss: Unifies two normally separate steps in a vector database search — turning a query into numbers, then finding the nearest stored entries — into one hardware design by recognizing that both steps reduce to the same dictionary-lookup operation; eliminates the data-format handoff between stages; 2.82 to 416x lower latency than CPU and GPU baselines.

papers.name: AIM
papers.gloss: Fixes an unexpected problem on chips that do math inside the memory: the bit patterns of rounded weights determine how much electrical current spikes inside the chip, and big spikes cause errors; AIM adds an extra training signal that steers weights toward bit patterns with fewer '1' bits, reducing voltage spikes by up to 69% and improving chip throughput by 1.15x.

connect: Every paper in this theme is ultimately solving the same physical constraint: the wires that carry numbers between memory chips and the math circuits are the bottleneck, not the math itself. Using smaller numbers is the discipline of packing more information into each wire transfer — whether by shrinking individual numbers, replacing math circuits with lookup tables, or skipping redundant values entirely — so that chips can run larger models faster without sitting idle, waiting for data to arrive.
